analysis.one_liner: Caps the total cost of consumer credit—interest plus fees—at 36% a year nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Banking Committee, dying there when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to make it illegal for any lender to charge consumers more than 36% a year in interest and fees combined—covering credit cards, overdraft loans, payday loans, car title loans, and online installment loans. It counts all charges, so lenders cannot dodge the cap by shifting interest into fees. Violating lenders would face criminal penalties, the debt itself would become unenforceable, state attorneys general could sue, and billing statements would have to show the total cost as a single 'FAIR' rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use high-cost credit: payday borrowers paying an average 400% annual interest, car title borrowers paying around 300%, bank customers hit with overdraft fees, and cardholders on subprime cards above 36%. Anyone whose illegal loan was made under the bill would get their principal, interest, and fees back.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday, overdraft, and high-interest card borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any creditor from extending consumer credit at a total fee-and-interest rate above 36%, with 'fee and interest rate' defined to include annual fees, cash advance fees, late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance premiums, and all ancillary products—closing the loopholes that let lenders evade state rate caps [S2][S3].

Makes payments on a violating loan null and void: the lender must return all principal, interest, charges, and fees, and the borrower can raise the violation as a defense in any collection lawsuit at any time [S3].

Imposes criminal penalties—up to 1 year in prison and a fine of the greater of triple the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation—and empowers state attorneys general to sue violators in federal court [S2][S3].

The bill's own findings state that consumers pay about $23.7 billion a year in high-cost overdraft loans and up to $8.1 billion for storefront and online payday loans, with average annual rates of 400% for payday loans, 300% for car title loans, and up to 3,500% for bank overdraft loans [S3].
Requires credit card statements to display the all-in cost as a rate labeled 'FAIR' instead of the traditional annual percentage rate, which excludes many fees [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday and car title lenders, banks that earn overdraft and deposit-advance revenue, and credit card issuers whose all-in costs exceed 36%—they would lose that revenue or have to stop offering the products. Some consumers who cannot qualify for cheaper credit could lose access to small-dollar loans entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, banks, and card issuers

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% cap on all fees can make short-term small-dollar lending unprofitable for legitimate lenders, which could leave borrowers with poor credit and no savings with no legal option at all in an emergency—the same objection made to the similar 2006 military lending cap, which lenders responded to with new workarounds.

The bill sets no exemptions the regulator could grant—the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is expressly barred from exempting anyone from the rate cap—leaving little flexibility if the cap cuts off credit to particular groups [S3].

Criminal penalties of prison time and fines up to $50,000 per violation, plus voiding of the underlying debt years later without a statute of limitations, is a far harsher enforcement regime than ordinary consumer credit law carries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of Americans paying triple-digit rates on payday and overdraft loans, the benefit is direct and large: rates capped at 36% and illegal loans voided. The real cost falls on borrowers at the highest risk, who might lose access to small-dollar credit entirely if lenders stop offering it rather than lend at 36%. Whether cheaper alternatives would emerge—credit unions, employer advances, or bank small-dollar products—is the key uncertainty; the bill encourages such alternatives in its findings but does not create them.

outcome.mechanism: Durbin introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Protecting Consumers from Unreasonable Credit Rates Act of 2012 on July 26, 2012, with Sens. Boxer, Merkley, and Whitehouse as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, and online lenders, and the banks collecting overdraft and high-rate card revenue, kept earning those fees because the bill never advanced. Borrowers paying 300–400% annual rates kept paying them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders kept their fee revenue

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 26, 2012, and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Barbara Boxer, Jeff Merkley, and Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tim Johnson
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Payday lending industry
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake against a 36% national rate cap and opposed similar federal cap proposals of the era.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no vote was ever taken, so the party split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: Their business model depends on rates averaging 400% and 300% annually, far above the cap; the bill would make those loans illegal and void the debts owed on them.
The bill counts overdraft and not-sufficient-funds fees toward the cap; the bill's findings put consumer overdraft costs at about $23.7 billion a year, revenue that would shrink sharply.

Most mainstream cards price under 36%, but subprime and fee-heavy cards exceed it once annual, cash advance, late, and over-limit fees are counted; those products would have to be repriced or withdrawn.
The bill's findings cite triple-digit rates on high-cost online installment loans as a target; all-in costs above 36% would be prohibited nationwide.
